body.en: This chapter builds the two sequence families EST II Math Level 2 tests — arithmetic (constant difference) and geometric (constant ratio) — and the surprising idea that an infinite sum can still equal a finite number, as long as the terms shrink fast enough.

A sequence \( a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots \) is arithmetic if consecutive terms differ by a constant \( d \): \( a_{n+1}=a_n+d \). Its explicit formula is

\[ a_n=a_1+(n-1)d. \]

body.en:
The sum of an arithmetic sequence's first \( n \) terms is

\[ S_n=\frac{n}{2}\big(a_1+a_n\big)=\frac{n}{2}\big(2a_1+(n-1)d\big). \]

label.en: Worked example 2.B — Sum an arithmetic series

body.en:
Find the sum of the first \( 12 \) terms of the sequence from Example 2.A (\( a_1=7,\,d=5 \)).

\[ S_{12}=\frac{12}{2}\big(2(7)+11(5)\big)=6(14+55)=6(69)=414. \]

A sequence is geometric if consecutive terms share a constant ratio \( r\neq0 \): \( a_{n+1}=r\,a_n \), with explicit formula

\[ a_n=a_1\,r^{\,n-1}. \]

label.en: Worked example 2.C — Find a geometric term

body.en:
A geometric sequence has \( a_1=4 \) and \( r=3 \). Find \( a_6 \).

\[ a_6=4\cdot3^{5}=4\cdot243=972. \]

For \( r\neq1 \), the sum of the first \( n \) terms of a geometric sequence is

\[ S_n=\frac{a_1(r^n-1)}{r-1}. \]

Write \( S_n=a_1+a_1r+a_1r^2+\cdots+a_1r^{n-1} \). Multiply by \( r \): \( rS_n=a_1r+a_1r^2+\cdots+a_1r^{n} \). Subtracting the first sum from the second cancels every middle term, leaving \( rS_n-S_n=a_1r^{n}-a_1 \), so \( S_n(r-1)=a_1(r^n-1) \). Since \( r\neq1 \), divide by \( r-1 \): \( S_n=\dfrac{a_1(r^n-1)}{r-1} \). \( \blacksquare \)

label.en: Worked example 2.D — Sum a geometric series

body.en:
If \( |r|<1 \), the infinite geometric series converges to

\[ S_\infty=\frac{a_1}{1-r}. \] If \( |r|\geq1 \) (and \( a_1\neq0 \)), the series diverges.

By Theorem 2.1, \( S_n=\dfrac{a_1}{1-r}(1-r^n) \). When \( |r|<1 \), repeated multiplication by a factor smaller than \( 1 \) in absolute value forces \( r^n\to0 \) as \( n\to\infty \), so \( S_n\to\dfrac{a_1}{1-r} \). When \( |r|\geq1 \), \( r^n \) never shrinks toward \( 0 \), so \( S_n \) never settles on a finite value. \( \blacksquare \)

label.en: Worked example 2.E — Sum an infinite geometric series

body.en:
Find \( 54+18+6+2+\cdots \).

Here \( a_1=54 \) and \( r=\tfrac13 \) (each term is a third of the last), and \( |r|=\tfrac13<1 \), so \[ S_\infty=\frac{54}{1-\tfrac13}=\frac{54}{\tfrac23}=81. \]

caption.en: Geometric sequence decay with first term a_1 = 54 and common ratio r = 1/3, with terms rapidly approaching 0.

body.en:
Common Ratio Sign: In alternating geometric series like \(12 - 6 + 3 - \cdots\), the common ratio is negative: \(r = -1/2\). Writing \(r = 1/2\) alters the denominator \(1 - r\) from \(1 - (-1/2) = 3/2\) to \(1/2\), resulting in an answer off by a factor of 3.

Number of Terms in Arithmetic Series: Never assume the number of terms \(n\) is the last number written. Always compute \(n = \dfrac{a_n - a_1}{d} + 1\).

Divergent Geometric Series: If \(|r| \geq 1\), the infinite sum \(S_\infty\) does not exist. Do not blindly use \(\dfrac{a_1}{1-r}\) on divergent series.

question.en: An arithmetic sequence has third term \(a_3 = 11\) and eighth term \(a_8 = 31\). Find the common difference \(d\), the first term \(a_1\), and the sum of the first 20 terms \(S_{20}\).
[Sequences & Series · Practice 2] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 4t + 4 \), evaluate \( g(6) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 32 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 6 \): \( g(6) = 4(6) + 4 = \mathbf{28} \). Setting \( 4t + 4 = 32 \) gives \( 4t = 28 \implies t = \mathbf{7} \).

question.en: [Sequences & Series · Practice 3] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 5t + 5 \), evaluate \( g(8) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 50 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 8 \): \( g(8) = 5(8) + 5 = \mathbf{45} \). Setting \( 5t + 5 = 50 \) gives \( 5t = 45 \implies t = \mathbf{9} \).

question.en: [Sequences & Series · Practice 4] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 6t + 6 \), evaluate \( g(10) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 72 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 10 \): \( g(10) = 6(10) + 6 = \mathbf{66} \). Setting \( 6t + 6 = 72 \) gives \( 6t = 66 \implies t = \mathbf{11} \).
